reddit has some pretty good guidelines on how to be a subreddit mod, and the wikis of most of them (and /r/TheoryofReddit) can probably help you there as well. Just, you know, actually abide by them.

The relationship between a mod and their community is wholly symbiotic; one cannot succeed without the other. If you're in a small community, which I imagine you are if you even have one yet, you're likely to be not a cop but a custodian and a tour guide. It's up to you to get the culture of the subverse rolling in the right direction (though only the community can get it started), and to make people interested in a) showing up and b) sticking around. Lots of community involvement, openness, basically being a regular joe except for where you take care of your folks and show that you're actually invested in making the place happen and stay happening.

For me, the hardest part is the interpersonal skill required. It's difficult to discipline people without coming off as either overly stern or a pansy, and unfortunately the mods getting press on reddit lately are coming off as total pricks – mostly because it's a lot easier to get noticed as a douchebag than a quiet servant. My own community's mods do a fantastic job of keeping things in line, mostly because we as a community don't really get out of line all that often. When we do, it's addressed, openly, with input from all sides before the mods do anything radical. Generally.

I guess it's kind of like being a parent, except if you're good at it you won't have four kids but hundreds or thousands. And also like being a parent, it's a thankless job and a bunch of your kids will hate you and if you screw up you'll get speared for it but when you do your job right you're invisible.

But with the right community, it's incredibly rewarding. The magic is just in getting one started.
